gameboard.campaignAllPlatinum: Platinum on every level: hats off!
gameboard.helpTitle: Facing Enigma, Turing didn't have the keys. Neither do you.

golden_3.title: You want a piece of Pi?

golden_4.title: WE HAVE TO GO BACK!
golden_4.description: Discover the sequence from the Lost series.

golden_8.title: Permission to enter the vacuum granted.

golden_9.title: Engage warp speed!
golden_9.description: Discover the speed of light constant.

legendary_Primer.title: Legendary twins
legendary_Primer.description: Make Primer legendary with twin primes of at least 4 digits (the score and the score + 2).

legendary_Split.title: Divide and conquer
legendary_Split.description: Make Split legendary with a multiple of 2520, divisible by every digit from 1 to 9.

legendary_Boost.title: Square and cube at once
legendary_Boost.description: Make Boost legendary with a sixth power (64, 729, 4096...).

legendary_Digit.title: Mirror, mirror on the wall
legendary_Digit.description: Make Digit legendary with a narcissistic number, equal to the sum of its digits each raised to the number of digits (153 = 1³ + 5³ + 3³).

legendary_Reduce.title: All in binary
legendary_Reduce.description: Make Reduce legendary with a power of 2 of at least 1024.

legendary_Align.title: Perfectly aligned
legendary_Align.description: Make Align legendary with a palindrome that has as many digits as the button's value.

legendary_Fiber.title: The sacred spiral
legendary_Fiber.description: Make Fiber legendary with a Fibonacci number that is also prime (13, 89, 233...).

legendary_Factor.title: Factorially yours
legendary_Factor.description: Make Factor legendary with a score that is exactly a factorial, from 4! = 24.

legendary_Cipher.title: Easy as 1, 2, 3
legendary_Cipher.description: Make Cipher legendary with at least 4 digits in a row, in ascending order (1234, 45678...).

legendary_Plus.title: Powers of ten
legendary_Plus.description: Make Plus legendary with a power of 10, from 100.

legendary_Minus.title: Broken record
legendary_Minus.description: Make Minus legendary with a score made only of the digit of its value, at least 3 digits long (777 for Minus 7).

legendary_Double.title: And then zeros
legendary_Double.description: Make Double legendary with its value followed by zeros, at least 3 digits long (500 for Double 5).

legendary_Half.title: A thousand times
legendary_Half.description: Make Half legendary with a multiple of 1000.

legendary_Mirror.title: Through the looking-glass
legendary_Mirror.description: Make Mirror legendary with a multiple of its mirror that is not a palindrome (8712 = 4 × 2178).

goodwin.name: Goodwin
goodwin.story: A doctor, he was certain he had proved that π equals 3.2. In 1897, he offered Indiana to make it law, and generously gave his discovery to the state’s schools. The House voted yes, unanimously. A math professor happened to be visiting the State House: the Senate postponed the vote. Indefinitely.
goodwin.jab: {clicks}. Indiana’s lawmakers would find you brilliant.

hanyecz.name: Hanyecz
hanyecz.story: On May 22, 2010, he paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas. It was the first known purchase made with bitcoin, and probably the most expensive pizzas in history. He says he regrets nothing.
hanyecz.jab: {clicks}. He traded a fortune for two pizzas, and he is still the smartest one in the room.

airy.name: Airy
airy.story: Astronomer Royal. In 1842, the government asked him whether Babbage’s calculating machine could be of any use. Answer: none. The funding was cut, and the computer would wait a century. A few years later, he would also be blamed for letting the discovery of Neptune slip away. A consistent man.
airy.jab: The machine’s report on your usefulness: about that of a horoscope.

preece.name: Preece
preece.story: An engineer at the British Post Office. In 1879, he told a parliamentary committee that the telephone was fine for Americans: the British had plenty of messenger boys. He was knighted anyway.
preece.jab: He didn’t see the telephone’s future. The machine doesn’t see yours.

stoll.name: Stoll
stoll.story: In 1986, he went after a hacker who was selling the KGB secrets stolen from his laboratory’s computers. In 1995, he mocked in Newsweek those who believed we would one day buy books on the Internet. Today, he sells Klein bottles. Online.
stoll.jab: He was wrong about the Internet, but he caught a spy. All you caught was this level.

stifel.name: Stifel
stifel.story: Mathematician and pastor. His calculations set the end of the world for October 19, 1533, at 8 a.m. His parishioners left everything to wait for it with him. At 8:01, the mood changed. He made up for it later: he is the one who coined the word “exponent”.
stifel.jab: His calculations were wrong, but his parishioners believed in them. Nobody believes in yours.

brahe.name: Brahe
brahe.story: At 20, he lost a piece of his nose in a duel over who was the better mathematician, and wore a brass prosthesis for the rest of his life. He is said to have died after refusing, out of politeness, to leave a banquet to go to the toilet. In between, he measured the sky precisely enough for Kepler to derive the laws of planetary motion.
brahe.jab: He lost his nose over a maths problem. You lost nothing: you had nothing to bet.

shanks.name: Shanks
shanks.story: He spent years computing π by hand, up to the 707th decimal place. He made a mistake at the 528th, and every digit after it was wrong. Nobody noticed for more than 70 years.
shanks.jab: He went more than five hundred decimals before his first mistake. You wouldn’t have got past the decimal point.

reichelt.name: Reichelt
reichelt.story: A tailor who invented a parachute suit. He had been allowed to test it from the Eiffel Tower, with a dummy. On February 4, 1912, in front of the cameras, he announced that he would be the dummy. He hesitated for forty seconds on the railing. The parachute never made up its mind.
reichelt.jab: At least he dared to jump. You hesitate in front of a button.

midgley.name: Midgley
midgley.story: He put lead in gasoline, then invented the CFCs that tore a hole in the ozone layer. To prove his lead was safe, he poured some on his hands in front of the press, a year after being treated for lead poisoning himself. One historian reckons no living being has changed Earth’s atmosphere as much.
midgley.jab: He changed the atmosphere of the whole planet. You haven’t even changed the atmosphere in this room.

brand.name: Brand
brand.story: An alchemist. Convinced that urine held the secret of gold, he boiled it down by the barrel. No gold, but a substance that glowed in the dark: phosphorus, one of the first chemical elements whose discoverer we know. History does not record what the neighbours thought.
brand.jab: He got light out of a chamber pot. Nobody has got anything out of you yet.

lowell.name: Lowell
lowell.story: He saw canals on Mars, dug by Martians. There were none. He also calculated where to look for an unknown planet: Pluto was found there, by sheer luck, because his calculations were wrong. Pluto starts with his initials. Since 2006, it is not even a planet anymore.
lowell.jab: With wrong calculations, he found a planet. With yours, nobody would find the way out.

millikan.name: Millikan
millikan.story: He spent ten years trying to prove Einstein wrong. He ended up proving him right, and won the Nobel Prize partly for it. Failing methodically can pay off.
millikan.jab: His failures earned him a Nobel Prize. Yours earn nobody anything.

fleming.name: Fleming
fleming.story: He went on holiday leaving his bacteria dishes lying around. When he came back, a mould had killed some of them: it was penicillin. His mess has saved millions of lives.
fleming.jab: His mess saved millions of lives. Yours interests nobody.

spencer.name: Spencer
spencer.story: He was working on a radar when the candy bar in his pocket began to melt. Instead of stepping away from the machine, he went to get some corn. The popcorn popped: the microwave oven was born.
spencer.jab: One candy bar was enough to inspire him. You would need the whole box.

greatbatch.name: Greatbatch
greatbatch.story: In 1956, he grabbed the wrong resistor from his box. Instead of recording heartbeats, his circuit started producing them. He turned it into one of the first implantable pacemakers. Millions of hearts beat thanks to a mix-up in a drawer.
greatbatch.jab: His worst mistake saved millions of hearts. Yours don’t make anyone’s heart beat.

lorenz.name: Lorenz
lorenz.story: To save time, he restarted his simulation halfway through, copying a printed value: 0.506 instead of 0.506127. His simulated weather went off in a completely different direction: he had just discovered the butterfly effect.
lorenz.jab: A butterfly flapping its wings can cause a storm. You can’t even cause a draught.

penzias_wilson.name: Penzias and Wilson
penzias_wilson.story: Their antenna picked up a noise they could not explain. They blamed the pigeons, cleaned up the droppings, chased the pigeons away. The noise remained: it was the echo of the Big Bang. Nobel Prize in 1978. The pigeons got nothing.
penzias_wilson.jab: Even background noise won them a Nobel Prize. You are just background noise.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.story: He claimed that women have fewer teeth than men. He was married, but never thought of counting. He still invented logic, without which no computer would work.
aristotle.jab: He was wrong about women’s teeth, and people believed him for two thousand years. Nobody would believe you for two minutes.

fermat.name: Fermat
fermat.story: He wrote in the margin of a book that he had a marvellous proof, but that the margin was too narrow to contain it. Mathematicians searched for more than three and a half centuries. The proof found in 1994 runs to more than a hundred pages. It needed a big margin.
fermat.jab: His margin was too narrow for his proof. Yours would fit on a stamp.

michelson.name: Michelson
michelson.story: A champion of precise measurement. In 1894, he judged it probable that the grand principles of physics were established, and quoted a colleague: all that was left was to hunt for the sixth decimal place. Eleven years later, Einstein published relativity, and everything had to be redone. Six decimals was cutting it a bit fine.
michelson.jab: He measured light with insane precision. To measure your speed, a calendar will do.

kelvin.name: Kelvin
kelvin.story: He gave his name to the absolute temperature scale. In 1896, he declined to join an aeronautical society: he had “not the smallest molecule of faith” in flight, except by balloon. Seven years later, the Wright brothers took off.
kelvin.jab: Even when he was wrong, he gave his name to something. Yours will be forgotten.

frege.name: Frege
frege.story: He spent years rebuilding arithmetic on logic alone. His second volume was going to press when Bertrand Russell wrote to him, very politely, that the whole thing rested on a contradiction. Frege added an appendix. He remains the father of modern logic.
frege.jab: A single letter shook his whole edifice. Yours would fall over at a comma.

hilbert.name: Hilbert
hilbert.story: In 1930, he proclaimed on the radio: “We must know, we will know.” The day before, in the same city, Kurt Gödel, aged 24, had announced that in any such system, some mathematical truths remain unprovable. Six years later, Turing drove the point home. The phrase is engraved on Hilbert’s tombstone.
hilbert.jab: Even his mistake is carved in stone. Yours doesn’t deserve a sticky note.

rutherford.name: Rutherford
rutherford.story: He discovered the atomic nucleus. In 1933, he declared that getting energy out of atoms was moonshine. The next day, Leó Szilárd read his speech in the newspaper, and came up with the chain reaction while waiting for a light to turn green.
rutherford.jab: His worst prediction sparked a revolution. Yours spark yawns.

hoyle.name: Hoyle
hoyle.story: He explained how stars make atoms. But he did not believe a universe could be born from an explosion, and in 1949, on the radio, he named that idea the “Big Bang”. The theory won. So did the name.
hoyle.jab: His mocking nickname ended up naming the origin of the universe. The machine is keeping yours to itself: it is too rude.

simon.name: Simon
simon.story: Nobel Prize in economics and Turing Award. In 1958, he predicted that a computer would be world chess champion within ten years. It took until 1997 for Deep Blue to beat the champion. Nearly thirty years late: in computing, that counts as on schedule.
simon.jab: He was thirty years behind his forecasts. You are forty years behind your times.

hoare.name: Hoare
hoare.story: He invented Quicksort, one of the most widely used sorting algorithms in the world. In 1965, he also invented the null reference, which he himself called his “billion-dollar mistake”. Programmers find the estimate modest.
hoare.jab: His mistake is worth a billion dollars. Yours are worth nothing.

papert.name: Papert
papert.story: He co-created Logo and its little turtle, which taught programming to generations of children. In 1966, he gave students a project for the summer: teach a computer to see. Sixty years later, summer isn’t quite over.
papert.jab: His little turtle taught programming to generations of children. It would be faster than you.

metcalfe.name: Metcalfe
metcalfe.story: He co-invented Ethernet, the network port on your computer. In 1995, he predicted the Internet would collapse the following year, and promised to eat his words if he was wrong. In 1997, on stage, he put his column in a blender and swallowed it. He, at least, keeps his word.
metcalfe.jab: He ate his words, and he had invented Ethernet. You could swallow a dictionary without inventing anything.

weizenbaum.name: Weizenbaum
weizenbaum.story: In 1966, he wrote ELIZA, one of the very first chatbots, to show that a machine can seem to understand without understanding anything. His secretary soon asked him to leave the room so she could talk to ELIZA in private. He spent the rest of his life warning against computers. He was right.
weizenbaum.jab: His secretary preferred talking to a machine. The machine understands why, now.

pythagoras.name: Pythagoras
pythagoras.story: Everyone knows his theorem, which is probably not his: the Babylonians were using it more than a thousand years earlier. He led a sect whose doctrine boils down to “all is number”, which believed in reincarnation and forbade eating beans. Legend has it that he was caught and killed by his enemies rather than flee across a bean field.
pythagoras.jab: He convinced disciples that all is number. You couldn’t convince a cat.

euclid.name: Euclid
euclid.story: His Elements served as the geometry textbook for more than two thousand years: after the Bible, it may be the most reprinted book in history. When King Ptolemy asked for a shortcut, he is said to have replied that there is no royal road to geometry.
euclid.jab: His book served for two thousand years. Your score won’t even last until tomorrow.

archimedes.name: Archimedes
archimedes.story: He pinned down π better than anyone before him, and worked out why ships float. Legend has it that he ran naked through Syracuse shouting “Eureka”, and that he was killed by a Roman soldier he had asked not to disturb his circles.

eratosthenes.name: Eratosthenes
eratosthenes.story: In the 3rd century BC, with shadows and a great deal of calculation, he measured the Earth’s circumference with remarkable accuracy. He ran the Library of Alexandria. Yet his contemporaries nicknamed him “Beta”: good at everything, first at nothing.
eratosthenes.jab: They called him the eternal runner-up. You haven’t even been ranked.

al_khwarizmi.name: Al-Khwarizmi
al_khwarizmi.story: A scholar in 9th-century Baghdad. His name, mangled into Latin, gave us the word “algorithm”, and the title of his book the word “algebra”. He also brought Indian numerals to the West, the ones we call Arabic.
al_khwarizmi.jab: His name became “algorithm”. Yours will become a forgotten password.

fibonacci.name: Fibonacci
fibonacci.story: In 1202, he showed European merchants how to count with Arabic numerals instead of Roman ones. In the same book, he worked out how many rabbits a single pair would produce in a year. The answer became the most famous sequence in mathematics. It even decided the size of every world in this game.
fibonacci.jab: His rabbits multiplied faster than your ideas. So does the next world: you already know by how much.

cardano.name: Cardano
cardano.story: Physician, mathematician and inveterate gambler, he wrote the first book on probability, with a chapter on how to cheat at dice. He published the formula for cubic equations that a rival had entrusted to him under oath. And he cast the horoscope of Jesus, which is thought to have landed him in prison.
cardano.jab: He cheated at dice and invented probability. Even cheating, you wouldn’t invent anything.

napier.name: Napier
napier.story: He invented logarithms, which saved astronomers years of calculation. His neighbours took him for a sorcerer. Legend has it that he unmasked a thief among his servants with a black rooster secretly covered in soot: only the culprit had not dared to touch it.
napier.jab: His neighbours took him for a sorcerer. Nobody will ever suspect you of magic.

descartes.name: Descartes
descartes.story: He is said to have invented coordinates by watching a fly on the ceiling, and summed up his philosophy in one sentence: “I think, therefore I am.” Since childhood, he had stayed in bed late in the morning. Queen Christina of Sweden brought him to Stockholm for lessons at 5 a.m., in the dead of winter. He died a few months later.
descartes.jab: He thought, therefore he was. With you, the machine is still waiting for the first part.

pascal.name: Pascal
pascal.story: At 19, to help his father with tax calculations, he invented one of the first calculating machines. He then laid the foundations of probability, before turning to religion, where he set out to prove that betting on the existence of God is the more reasonable choice. A programming language bears his name.
pascal.jab: At 19, he built a calculating machine. At your age, you struggle to use this one.

newton.name: Newton
newton.story: He explained falling apples and the motion of the planets with the same law. He then ran the Royal Mint, and lost a fortune on the stock market in the South Sea Bubble. He wrote more pages on alchemy and the prophecies of the Bible than on physics.
newton.jab: One apple was enough for him to understand the universe. A whole orchard wouldn’t help you.

leibniz.name: Leibniz
leibniz.story: Independently of Newton, he invented calculus, with the notation still in use today. To settle who came first, the Royal Society set up a committee, whose report was secretly written by… Newton. Leibniz also worked out binary arithmetic, the one every machine uses.
leibniz.jab: He reduced everything to zeros and ones. For you, a single digit will do.

euler.name: Euler
euler.story: He is said to be the most prolific mathematician ever: his collected works run to more than eighty volumes. When he went almost blind, he carried on by dictating, and produced even more. He also proved that the seven bridges of Königsberg could not each be crossed exactly once, founding graph theory along the way.
euler.jab: Almost blind, he produced more than anyone. You, with your eyes wide open, produce this.

gauss.name: Gauss
gauss.story: The prince of mathematicians. At 18, he found how to construct a 17-sided polygon with ruler and compass, the first progress on such constructions since Antiquity. He was so proud of it that he is said to have wanted it on his tombstone. The stonemason supposedly refused: with 17 sides, it would look like a circle.
gauss.jab: He wanted a polygon on his tombstone. On yours, a dot will do.

germain.name: Sophie Germain
germain.story: Women were not admitted to the École Polytechnique: she got hold of the lecture notes, and sent in her work under the name “Monsieur Le Blanc”. She went on to correspond with Gauss under that name. When Napoleon’s troops occupied Gauss’s town, she asked a French general to look after him. Gauss, puzzled by this unknown name, soon learned who his correspondent was.
germain.jab: She had to pass herself off as a man to be taken seriously. Even in disguise, you wouldn’t manage.

jacquard.name: Jacquard
jacquard.story: In the early 19th century, he invented a loom driven by punched cards: each hole decides a thread. The Lyon silk weavers, fearing for their jobs, burned his machines. His cards were later meant to program Babbage’s engine, then fed calculating machines for nearly a century.
jacquard.jab: The machine runs on holes too. In your reasoning, mostly.

babbage.name: Babbage
babbage.story: He designed the first programmable calculating machine, a century before computers. For lack of money, and partly because of a certain Airy, he never finished it. He also waged a crusade against street musicians, whom he accused of stealing a quarter of his working power. They came to play under his windows on purpose.
babbage.jab: The musicians’ noise stole a quarter of his genius. You don’t have a quarter left to steal.

galois.name: Galois
galois.story: Twice rejected by the École Polytechnique, he invented a theory that tells which equations have a formula for their solutions, and which never will. He died in a duel at 20. The night before, in a letter to a friend summing up his discoveries, he wrote: “I have not the time.” It took mathematicians years to understand what he had found.
galois.jab: In one night, he summed up a mathematical revolution. In one night, you couldn’t sum up this level.

lovelace.name: Lovelace
lovelace.story: The daughter of the poet Byron, she wrote in 1843 what is considered the first computer program, for a Babbage machine that never existed. She understood before anyone else that a machine could handle more than numbers, music for instance. She also devised a mathematical system for betting on horse races. It left her deep in debt.
lovelace.jab: She wrote the first program for a machine that didn’t exist. You have a machine right in front of you, and you don’t know what to do with it.

boole.name: Boole
boole.story: A shoemaker’s son and a self-taught mathematician, he reduced logic to an algebra where everything is 0 or 1, false or true. Every button in this game, green or red, obeys his laws. He is said to have died after lecturing soaked by the rain. His wife, convinced that the remedy should resemble the cause, supposedly doused him with cold water.
boole.jab: He reduced everything to true or false. For you, the machine has already decided: false.

cantor.name: Cantor
cantor.story: He proved that there are several infinities, and that some are bigger than others. Some of his colleagues cried scandal, and one of them reportedly called him a “corrupter of youth”. Hilbert, for his part, declared that no one would drive us from the paradise Cantor had created.
cantor.jab: The machine counted your mistakes. It has just discovered a new infinity.

hollerith.name: Hollerith
hollerith.story: It took nearly eight years to process the 1880 American census. For the 1890 one, he invented a punched-card machine: the first count came in within weeks. His small company merged with others to become IBM.
hollerith.jab: He counted sixty-two million Americans faster than you count your clicks.

russell.name: Russell
russell.story: With Whitehead, he wrote the Principia Mathematica to found mathematics on logic alone. It takes them hundreds of pages to establish that 1 + 1 = 2, a result they deem “occasionally useful”. Later, this logician won the Nobel Prize… in literature.
russell.jab: It took him hundreds of pages to prove that 1 + 1 = 2. You are still not convinced.

hardy.name: Hardy
hardy.story: He was glad that number theory was of no use, least of all for waging war. It now protects every online payment and every military secret. Before crossing a stormy sea, he is said to have sent a postcard claiming he had proved the Riemann hypothesis: God, who hated him, would never let him die with such glory.
hardy.jab: His mathematics were never meant to be useful. Yours have kept that promise.

ramanujan.name: Ramanujan
ramanujan.story: A clerk in Madras with no degree, he sent Hardy pages of formulas. Hardy first suspected a fraud, then concluded they had to be true, because no one would have had the imagination to invent them. One day, Hardy visited him by taxi and found its number, 1729, rather dull. Ramanujan replied at once: it is the smallest number expressible as the sum of two cubes in two different ways.
ramanujan.jab: He saw wonders in a taxi number. You look at this score and see nothing.

noether.name: Emmy Noether
noether.story: Women were not allowed to teach at the University of Göttingen: for years, her lectures were announced under Hilbert’s name. Yet she proved the theorem that links the symmetries of the universe to its conservation laws, one of the pillars of modern physics. Einstein wrote that, in the judgment of the greatest living mathematicians, she was the most significant creative mathematical genius since higher education opened to women.
noether.jab: She changed physics without even being allowed her own name. You have yours, and it doesn’t help.

godel.name: Gödel
godel.story: At 24, he proved that every consistent and sufficiently rich mathematical system contains truths that cannot be proved. To become an American citizen, he studied the Constitution, and wanted to explain to the judge a flaw he had found that would allow a dictatorship. The judge hastily changed the subject. For Einstein’s 70th birthday, he gave him a universe where time travel is possible.
godel.jab: He proved that some truths escape all proof. Your talent, for instance.

rejewski.name: Rejewski
rejewski.story: In 1932, this young Polish mathematician reconstructed the wiring of Enigma using permutation theory and a spy’s documents, without ever having seen the military machine. His team read German messages for years. In July 1939, Poland handed everything to the British and the French: the methods, and copies of Enigma.
rejewski.jab: Facing Enigma, Turing didn’t have the keys: he and his team are the ones who handed them over. Nobody will hand them to you.

shannon.name: Shannon
shannon.story: At 21, his master’s thesis showed that Boolean algebra could make electrical circuits compute: it has been called possibly the most important master’s thesis of the century. Eleven years later, he founded information theory and made the bit its unit. In the 1950s, he rode a unicycle through the halls of Bell Labs, juggling.
shannon.jab: He thought while juggling on a unicycle. You, sitting on a chair, manage neither.

zuse.name: Zuse
zuse.story: An aeronautical engineer tired of calculating by hand, he built his first machines in his parents’ living room in Berlin. In 1941, his Z3 became the first working programmable computer. He also designed the first high-level programming language, years ahead of everyone else.
zuse.jab: He built a computer in a living room. You, in yours, can’t even work this one.

flowers.name: Flowers
flowers.story: An engineer at the British Post Office, like Preece before him, he built Colossus, the first programmable electronic machine, to break the German high command’s codes, and paid for part of it out of his own pocket. After the war, almost everything was destroyed and classified. When he asked for a loan to build a computer, the bank refused: it did not believe such a machine could work.
flowers.jab: Nobody believed in him, and he was right. Nobody believes in you either.

von_neumann.name: von Neumann
von_neumann.story: He gave his name to the architecture of nearly every computer, co-founded game theory, and could reportedly calculate in his head faster than the first machines. Behind the wheel, however, he was a disaster: after one accident, he supposedly explained that the trees on his right were passing by in orderly fashion when one of them stepped into his path.
von_neumann.jab: He calculated faster than machines. You? The machine is the one waiting for you.

bartik.name: Bartik
bartik.story: In 1946, six women programmed ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic computer, without any manual, from wiring diagrams alone, plugging cables by hand. On the day of the triumphant demonstration, the machine worked perfectly. The programmers were not invited to the celebration dinner.
bartik.jab: They programmed a machine without any manual. You, with no instructions, click at random.

hopper.name: Hopper
hopper.story: She wrote one of the first compilers and inspired COBOL, which still runs the banks. In 1947, her team found a moth stuck in a relay and taped it into the logbook: “first actual case of bug being found”. To explain a nanosecond, she handed out pieces of wire thirty centimetres long. The Navy had to call her back from retirement, and she served until 79.
hopper.jab: Her team removed bugs with tweezers. You are one.

hamming.name: Hamming
hamming.story: At Bell Labs, the machines stopped at the slightest error, and at weekends nobody was there to restart them. Fed up with finding his work lost two Mondays in a row, he invented codes that correct their own errors. Their descendants now protect computer memories and the messages of space probes.
hamming.jab: He knew how to correct machines’ errors. Yours would need a far more powerful code.

minsky.name: Minsky
minsky.story: A pioneer of artificial intelligence, he built one of the first artificial neural networks as early as 1951. Between two theories of the mind, he invented the confocal microscope, now found in biology labs all over the world. He also imagined a machine whose only function is to switch itself off as soon as it is switched on.
minsky.jab: He imagined a machine that switches itself off as soon as it is switched on. You look a lot like it.

backus.name: Backus
backus.story: Programming in machine language bored him deeply. So in 1957, with his team at IBM, he created Fortran, the first widely used high-level language, which still computes the weather on supercomputers. He maintained that most of his work came from being lazy.
backus.jab: His laziness gave the world Fortran. Yours only gave this score.

mccarthy.name: McCarthy
mccarthy.story: In 1955, he coined the term “artificial intelligence” for a summer workshop. Three years later, he created Lisp, one of the oldest languages still in use, inventing garbage collection along the way, which frees memory on its own. As early as 1961, he predicted that computing power would one day be rented as a public utility, like the telephone: the cloud.
mccarthy.jab: He gave artificial intelligence a name. For yours, we are still looking.

dijkstra.name: Dijkstra
dijkstra.story: In 1956, at a café terrace in Amsterdam, without pen or paper, he found the shortest-path algorithm in twenty minutes. GPS systems still draw on it. He did not mince his words: in his view, teaching BASIC mutilated students’ minds beyond hope of regeneration.
dijkstra.jab: He solved his problems in his head, at a café terrace. You need a screen, some buttons, and a bit of luck.

johnson.name: Katherine Johnson
johnson.story: A NASA mathematician, she calculated by hand the trajectories of the first American space missions. In 1962, before becoming the first American in orbit, John Glenn demanded that she check the computer’s calculations: if she said they were good, he was ready to go. She confirmed. He went.
johnson.jab: An astronaut trusted his life to her calculations. Nobody would trust you with a calculator.

knuth.name: Knuth
knuth.story: In 1962, he began The Art of Computer Programming, a book that would grow into a seven-volume project. He is still at it. Unhappy with the typesetting of the new edition of his second volume, he spent eight years inventing TeX, which still typesets most mathematics papers. To the first person who finds each mistake in his books, he sends a “hexadecimal dollar” worth $2.56, once by cheque, now as a certificate from his imaginary bank.
knuth.jab: He pays people who find his mistakes. With yours, he would be broke.

moore.name: Moore
moore.story: In 1965, he predicted that the number of transistors on a chip would double at regular intervals. He thought it would hold for about ten years. It held for half a century. Meanwhile, he co-founded Intel to see to it himself.
moore.jab: The transistors on a chip used to double every two years. With you, we are still waiting for the first doubling.

engelbart.name: Engelbart
engelbart.story: In 1968, in a single ninety-minute demonstration, he presented the mouse, hypertext links, word processing, videoconferencing and several people editing the same document. The audience rose to give him a standing ovation. The mouse earned him almost nothing: the patent expired before it caught on.
engelbart.jab: He invented the mouse to change the world. You use it to click at random.

thompson.name: Thompson
thompson.story: In 1969, his wife went on a three-week holiday with their son. He took the opportunity to write, one piece a week, what his operating system was missing: Unix, from which macOS and the iPhone descend, and which inspired Linux and Android. He reportedly said that one of his most productive days was the one when he threw away a thousand lines of code.
thompson.jab: He finished Unix during his wife’s holiday. You, during yours, play this.

ritchie.name: Ritchie
ritchie.story: He created the C language, in which most operating systems are still written, and rewrote Unix with Thompson. He himself found his language quirky and flawed, while acknowledging its enormous success. He was never officially a doctor: he had not handed in the bound copy of his thesis to the library.
ritchie.jab: He didn’t even bother to collect his degree. You will never be given one.

kay.name: Kay
kay.story: In 1972, he sketched the Dynabook, a flat, portable computer for children: the tablet, nearly forty years before the iPad. At Xerox, he helped invent windows and object-oriented programming. Xerox did almost nothing with it, and Steve Jobs, on a visit, left with ideas. His motto: the best way to predict the future is to invent it.
kay.jab: He saw the future forty years ahead. You can’t see the next click.

cerf.name: Cerf
cerf.story: With Bob Kahn, he designed in 1974 the protocol that connects all the world’s networks: the Internet. In 1977, he provided for 4.3 billion addresses, thinking that would be plenty for an experiment. The experiment grew a little. He then spent more than twenty years as Google’s “Chief Internet Evangelist”.
cerf.jab: He connected the whole world. You can’t connect two ideas.

diffie_hellman.name: Diffie and Hellman
diffie_hellman.story: In 1976, they showed how two strangers can agree on a secret while talking in public, without anyone else being able to discover it. This is public-key cryptography: the padlock on every website depends on it. The British secret services had found it a few years earlier, but were not allowed to tell anyone.
diffie_hellman.jab: They knew how to share a secret in front of everyone. Yours is well kept: nobody knows how you succeeded. Not even you.

lamport.name: Lamport
lamport.story: He laid the foundations of distributed systems, which run the cloud, and created LaTeX. To explain his consensus algorithm, he presented it as the story of an imaginary parliament on the Greek island of Paxos. Nobody got the joke, and the paper waited eight years to be published. He eventually received the Turing Award.
lamport.jab: His jokes were too subtle for his readers. You are the joke.

stroustrup.name: Stroustrup
stroustrup.story: In 1985, he released C++, which runs video games, browsers and financial markets. His critics find it too complicated. He answered them once and for all: there are only two kinds of languages, the ones people complain about and the ones nobody uses.
stroustrup.jab: The machine complains about you a lot. That doesn’t make you useful.

berners_lee.name: Berners-Lee
berners_lee.story: In 1989, at CERN, he proposed a system for researchers to share documents. His boss scribbled on the proposal: “vague but exciting”. It was the Web. He refused to patent it and gave it to the whole world for free. One of his regrets: the two slashes in addresses, which serve no purpose.
berners_lee.jab: He gave the Web to all of humanity. You use it for this.

torvalds.name: Torvalds
torvalds.story: In 1991, a Finnish student announced a small operating system on a forum, “just a hobby, won’t be big and professional”. It was Linux: it runs Android, most servers and all five hundred of the world’s most powerful supercomputers. In 2005, he wrote Git in a few weeks. He jokingly claims he named both projects after himself: Linux, and git, British slang for an unpleasant person.
torvalds.jab: His hobby runs the planet. Yours is this.

nakamoto.name: Nakamoto
nakamoto.story: In 2008, an unknown person published nine pages describing a currency with no bank and no state: bitcoin. Two years later, they vanished without ever revealing their identity, leaving behind, by some estimates, about a million bitcoins that have never been touched. Without them, Hanyecz would never have paid so much for his pizzas.
nakamoto.jab: They stayed anonymous by choice. You, out of necessity.

hinton.name: Hinton
hinton.story: For decades, almost nobody believed in artificial neural networks. He persisted. In 2012, his students crushed an image recognition contest, and everything changed: modern artificial intelligence was born. A Turing Award winner, he left Google in 2023 to warn the world about the dangers of what he had created, then received the Nobel Prize in physics in 2024.
hinton.jab: He taught machines to learn. The machine has learned a lot by watching you. Mostly what not to do.

turing.name: Turing
turing.story: In 1936, at 23, to prove that some problems can never be solved by computation, he imagined a machine able to carry out any computation: the computer, on paper. During the war, at Bletchley Park, he helped break Enigma. In 1950, he asked the question that haunts this game: can machines think? His face is now on the £50 note.
turing.jab: He wondered whether machines could think. After all these levels, the machine is asking the same question about you.

settings.resetWarning: All medals and achievements will be permanently lost.
